basics: A skeleton is a load-bearing frame of stiff elements (bones) connected at joints. Anatomists split the 206 adult bones into two sets. The axial skeleton lies along the body's central axis (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum) and mainly protects organs. The appendicular skeleton is everything that hangs off that axis: the limbs plus the two girdles, partial rings of bone that anchor the limbs to the trunk. The pectoral girdle (clavicle and scapula) carries the arm; the pelvic girdle (two hip bones) carries the leg. Because appendicular bones are joined by mobile joints and pulled by large muscles, their main job is movement rather than protection, which is what the slide's 'more related to movements' means. Left unsaid: the two girdles differ greatly in mobility. The pectoral girdle floats on muscles and never touches the spine; the pelvic girdle is locked to the sacrum.

basics: Counting bones is bookkeeping, but it forces you to notice the structure. Each side has one bone in the arm (humerus), two in the forearm (ulna, radius), eight small wrist bones (carpals), five palm bones (metacarpals) and 14 finger bones (phalanges): 30 per upper limb. The lower limb mirrors it: femur, patella, tibia, fibula, seven ankle bones (tarsals), five metatarsals and 14 phalanges, again 30. Add the girdles (clavicle and scapula on each side; one hip bone on each side) and you reach 126, against 80 in the axial skeleton. The hip bone counts as one because three childhood bones (ilium, ischium, pubis) fuse. Fourteen phalanges per hand comes from three bones in each of four fingers plus two in the thumb. The slide's 'Phalange' is a back-formation; the singular is phalanx.

basics: A girdle is a partial ring of bone connecting a limb to the trunk. The pectoral girdle on each side is only two bones: the clavicle (collarbone) in front and the scapula (shoulder blade) behind. Its single bony contact with the axial skeleton is where the clavicle meets the manubrium of the sternum (sternoclavicular joint); the clavicle then meets the scapula's acromion (acromioclavicular joint), and the scapula's shallow socket receives the humerus (glenohumeral or shoulder joint). The scapula itself is not attached to ribs or spine by bone at all; it is slung in muscles. This trades stability for a huge range of motion, which is why the shoulder dislocates more readily than the hip. The slide's 'shoulder joint' means the glenohumeral joint specifically. It does not mention the acromioclavicular joint, the third joint of the system, nor that the pectoral girdle is stabilised by muscles from the vertebral column and ribs.

basics: The clavicle is a slender S-shaped strut lying horizontally just under the skin above the first rib. Its job is mechanical: it props the shoulder out to the side and transmits force from the upper limb to the trunk, which is why a fall on an outstretched arm often breaks it at the junction of its two curves. Read the slide's labels as joint surfaces and attachment sites. The rounded medial (sternal) end has a facet for the sternum; the flat lateral (acromial) end has a facet for the acromion. On the underside, the conoid tubercle and trapezoid line anchor the two coracoclavicular ligaments that tie the clavicle to the coracoid process of the scapula, and the costal tuberosity (Tortora's 'impression for the costoclavicular ligament') anchors the ligament to the first rib. The subclavian groove is where the subclavius muscle lies. A facet is simply a small smooth articular surface.

basics: The scapula is a flat triangular plate lying over the back of ribs 2-7, connected to the trunk only through the clavicle and by muscles. Its landmarks are named by geometry: three borders (superior, medial, lateral), three angles (superior, inferior, lateral), and a ridge across the back, the spine, that ends laterally in the acromion, the bony tip of the shoulder. The spine divides the back into a supraspinous fossa above and an infraspinous fossa below; the front is one hollow, the subscapular fossa. A fossa is a shallow depression, and each is the origin of a muscle named for it: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis. With teres minor these four form the rotator cuff, the slide's 'SITS'. Their tendons blend into a sleeve around the glenohumeral joint, pulling the humeral head into the shallow glenoid cavity to keep the joint stable. The coracoid process, a hook on the front, anchors biceps, coracobrachialis and pectoralis minor.

basics: The humerus is the single bone of the arm (anatomically, 'arm' means shoulder to elbow only). Its proximal end is a half-sphere head that sits in the scapula's glenoid cavity. Two 'necks' follow, and the slide asks you to distinguish them. The anatomical neck is the faint oblique groove immediately around the rim of the head: the scar of the growth plate, i.e. the true boundary of the joint surface. The surgical neck is the narrowing below the two tubercles where the wide upper end tapers into the shaft; it is called surgical because that is where the bone usually breaks. The greater and lesser tubercles are muscle attachments, with the intertubercular (bicipital) groove between them carrying the long biceps tendon. Halfway down, the deltoid tuberosity is where the deltoid pulls. Distally the bone flattens into two joint surfaces, capitulum and trochlea, with fossae above them that receive the forearm bones as the elbow bends or straightens.

basics: The lower end of the humerus is built to form two joints side by side. Laterally the capitulum ('little head') is a rounded knob on which the cup-shaped head of the radius rolls and spins. Medially the trochlea ('pulley') is a spool-shaped surface gripped by the ulna's trochlear notch, which makes the elbow a true hinge. A condyle is any rounded articular knob; an epicondyle is the rough bump above it that takes no part in the joint but gives muscles an anchor: the medial epicondyle for the forearm flexors, the lateral for the extensors. The fossae are hollows that let the forearm bones swing fully: the coronoid and radial fossae in front receive the ulna's coronoid process and the radial head when you flex; the olecranon fossa behind receives the ulna's olecranon when you extend. The supracondylar ridges simply extend those muscle attachments up the shaft.

basics: Two parallel bones span the forearm. The ulna is the longer medial one (little-finger side); the radius is lateral (thumb side). Their shapes are opposite: the ulna is thick at the elbow, where its hook, the olecranon behind and coronoid process in front, clamps round the humeral trochlea, and thin at the wrist; the radius is thin at the elbow (a small disc-shaped head) and wide at the wrist, where it carries most of the hand. The two bones touch at both ends: proximally the radial head sits in the ulna's radial notch, distally the ulnar head sits in the radius's ulnar notch. These proximal and distal radioulnar joints let the radius pivot round the ulna, which is how you turn the palm down (pronation) and up (supination). Between the shafts stretches the interosseous membrane, a fibrous sheet that ties the bones together and gives deep muscles attachment. The styloid processes are the pointed distal tips felt at the wrist.

basics: The elbow is really two articulations inside one capsule. The humero-ulnar part is a hinge: the spool-shaped trochlea of the humerus fits into the ulna's trochlear notch, allowing only flexion and extension. The humero-radial part is the radial head resting on the capitulum, a shallow ball-in-cup that lets the radius both hinge alongside the ulna and spin on its own axis. That spin is used by a third, separate joint, the proximal radioulnar joint, where the rim of the radial head turns inside the radial notch of the ulna, held in place by a ring-shaped annular ligament. This is a pivot joint and, with its partner at the wrist, produces pronation and supination without moving the elbow hinge. The slide gives only the bony surfaces; the ligaments that keep those surfaces together (ulnar and radial collateral, annular) are in Tortora section 9.11.

basics: The hand has three tiers. Nearest the forearm are eight carpal bones packed in two rows of four; they slide slightly on one another (intercarpal joints), giving the wrist cushioned flexibility. The wrist (radiocarpal) joint proper is between the broad end of the radius and the proximal carpal row, mainly the scaphoid and lunate. Next come five metacarpals forming the palm, numbered 1-5 from the thumb; each has a base, shaft and head, and the heads are the knuckles. Distal to them are 14 phalanges: two in the thumb, three (proximal, middle, distal) in each finger. Joint names are built from the bones they connect: carpometacarpal, metacarpophalangeal (MCP, the knuckle), proximal and distal interphalangeal (PIP, DIP). The small sesamoid bones near the thumb are bones that form inside tendons, like the patella. 'Pollex' is Latin for thumb; fingers are index, middle, ring and little.

basics: The pelvis is a bony basin made of the two hip bones plus the sacrum and coccyx of the spine. Each hip bone is one fused unit in an adult but is described as three bones that meet in the socket for the femur (acetabulum): the ilium (the fan-shaped wing you rest your hands on), the ischium (the bone you sit on) and the pubis (in front). The hip bones meet each other only in front, at the pubic symphysis, a pad of fibrocartilage (the slide's 'interpubic disc'); behind, each meets the sacrum at a sacroiliac joint. The slide's labels are the palpable bumps clinicians use: the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) at the front end of the iliac crest, the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) just below it, and the ischial tuberosity, the thick roughened knob that takes your weight when sitting. The pubis has a body and two branches (rami) that with the ischium ring the obturator foramen, the largest hole in the skeleton, mostly sealed by membrane.

basics: Anatomists split the basin into an upper and a lower part by drawing an oblique plane through the pelvic inlet (pelvic brim): from the sacral promontory at the back, along the arcuate line of each ilium and the pecten pubis, to the top of the pubic symphysis in front. Above that plane is the greater or 'false' pelvis, really part of the lower abdomen, bounded by the flaring iliac wings and the abdominal wall; it holds intestines and, in women, the uterus. Below the plane is the lesser or 'true' pelvis, the ring of bone enclosing the pelvic cavity (bladder, rectum, reproductive organs). It has an inlet above and an outlet below, the outlet closed by the pelvic floor muscles. The pelvic axis is the curved line from the centre of the inlet to the centre of the outlet, the path a baby's head follows during birth, which is why obstetricians measure these planes (pelvimetry) and why the female pelvis is wider and shallower (Table 8.1).

basics: The femur is the longest and strongest bone, running from hip to knee. Its head is about two-thirds of a sphere and sits deep in the acetabulum; a small pit on the head, the fovea capitis, is where the ligamentum teres (ligament of the head of the femur) attaches, carrying a small artery into the head. The angled neck joins head to shaft; an elderly 'broken hip' is usually a fracture here. The greater and lesser trochanters are large muscle attachments at the top of the shaft, joined in front by the intertrochanteric line and behind by the crest. Down the back of the shaft runs the linea aspera ('rough line'), a ridge for thigh muscles. The distal end widens into medial and lateral condyles that rest on the tibia, with the patellar surface between them in front. The patella is a sesamoid bone in the quadriceps tendon: base up, apex down, two facets behind.

basics: The knee is where the femur's two condyles rest on the flat top (plateau) of the tibia, whose corresponding medial and lateral condyles are slightly cupped and deepened by two crescents of fibrocartilage, the menisci. The patella glides in the groove on the front of the femur (the patellar surface), so the joint is really three joints in one capsule, two tibiofemoral and one patellofemoral: hence 'three bones'. The fibula is not part of the knee: it does not reach the femur, and its head simply articulates with the side of the lateral tibial condyle at the superior (proximal) tibiofibular joint. The tibial tuberosity below the plateau is where the patellar ligament (the continuation of the quadriceps tendon) inserts, so straightening the knee pulls the tibia through this bump. Because the surfaces are so flat, the knee relies on ligaments, collateral ones at the sides and the cruciate pair inside, for stability.

basics: The leg (anatomically, knee to ankle) has two bones like the forearm, but the division of labour is more extreme. The tibia is the big medial bone: it takes the body's weight from the femur and its sharp anterior border is the shin you can feel. The fibula is a slender lateral splint that bears no weight and does not even reach the knee joint; it exists to anchor muscles and to form the outer wall of the ankle. The two are joined at their ends (proximal and distal tibiofibular joints) and along their length by an interosseous membrane. At the ankle the talus, the top bone of the foot, is gripped like a tenon in a mortise: the medial malleolus of the tibia inside and the lateral malleolus of the fibula outside are the bumps at your ankle. This is a hinge, giving dorsiflexion and plantar flexion only; side-to-side tilting happens lower, between the tarsal bones.

basics: If the foot bones lay flat, every step would slam bone onto ground. Instead ligaments and tendons hold the tarsals and metatarsals in curved arrangements, so the foot touches down only at the heel, the outer edge and the ball. Think of them as springy bridges. The longitudinal arch runs heel to toes and has a high medial part (calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms, medial three metatarsals) and a low lateral part (calcaneus, cuboid, lateral two metatarsals). The transverse arch runs across the foot through the cuneiforms, cuboid and metatarsal bases. When weight is applied the arches flatten slightly, stretching their ligaments and storing elastic energy, then recoil at toe-off: this is the shock absorption and 'leverage' the slide mentions. It also spreads load between hard bone and the soft pads of the sole. If the supporting ligaments weaken the medial arch drops (flatfoot); the arches are normally complete by age 12-13.

title: Bone formation

refs.section_title: Bone Formation

basics: Bone tissue is a composite: a protein scaffold (mostly collagen) stiffened by crystals of calcium phosphate. It is made by osteoblasts, which secrete the scaffold and then trigger its mineralisation, and dismantled by osteoclasts. 'Ossification' (or osteogenesis) is simply the word for turning some other tissue into bone. The slide lists when this happens: building the embryonic skeleton, lengthening and thickening bones during growth, the continuous swap of old bone for new in adults (remodeling), and mending fractures. Whatever the occasion, there are only two recipes, distinguished by the starting material. In intramembranous ossification bone forms directly within a sheet of embryonic connective tissue (mesenchyme). In endochondral ossification ('within cartilage') a hyaline-cartilage model of the bone is built first and then progressively replaced by bone. The finished bone looks the same either way; only the route differs. Both begin around week 6 of embryonic life.

title: Intramembranous ossification

basics: This is the simpler route: bone forms directly inside a membrane-like sheet of mesenchyme, with no cartilage stage. Step 1: at the future bone site mesenchymal cells cluster and mature into osteoblasts, which start secreting organic matrix; the cluster is the ossification centre. Step 2: calcium salts precipitate in the matrix (calcification), and the osteoblasts, now walled in, become osteocytes sitting in small chambers (lacunae) linked by tiny canals. Step 3: the calcified matrix grows into a lattice of struts (trabeculae) around blood vessels, i.e. spongy bone; the vascular tissue inside becomes red marrow. Step 4: the mesenchyme at the surface condenses into the periosteum, and a thin shell of compact bone forms beneath it while spongy bone stays in the centre. This route makes the flat bones of the skull roof, most facial bones, the mandible and the medial clavicle. The fontanels ('soft spots') of a baby's skull are membrane not yet ossified.

basics: Most bones, including all the long bones of the limbs, are first built as a scale model in hyaline cartilage and then converted to bone from the inside out. Mesenchyme condenses into chondroblasts that secrete a cartilage model wrapped in a perichondrium; the model grows in length by cell division inside it and in thickness by adding cartilage at its surface. Chondrocytes in the middle enlarge and the matrix around them calcifies, starving them; a nutrient artery invades this dying centre, the perichondrium becomes a bone-forming periosteum, and osteoblasts lay bone on the calcified cartilage: the primary ossification centre in the shaft (diaphysis). Osteoclasts then hollow the shaft into a medullary cavity. Around birth, secondary centres appear in the bone ends (epiphyses) and ossify outward, leaving cartilage in two places only: the articular cartilage on the joint surface and the epiphyseal plate between shaft and end, from which the bone will keep growing in length.

title: Bone growth in length

basics: A long bone cannot lengthen by adding bone at its ends, because the ends are already capped by joint cartilage. Instead growth happens at a disc of hyaline cartilage, the epiphyseal (growth) plate, trapped between shaft and end. Read the plate from the epiphysis downward. The resting zone anchors the plate to the epiphysis. In the proliferating zone chondrocytes divide in stacked columns, pushing the epiphysis away from the shaft: this is where length is generated, by cartilage, not bone. In the hypertrophic zone those cells swell and mature. In the calcified zone the matrix mineralises, the cells die, and osteoclasts and blood vessels from the shaft invade; osteoblasts then deposit bone on the calcified scaffold, so the shaft side of the plate is continuously converted into 'new diaphysis'. The plate keeps the same thickness while the bone lengthens. At the end of puberty sex hormones stop the divisions, the plate ossifies into an epiphyseal line, and growth in height ends.

title: Bone growth in thickness

basics: Widening a bone is appositional growth: new layers are added to the outside while the inside is hollowed, so the bone gets wider without becoming solid and heavy. The engine is the periosteum, whose inner layer holds osteoprogenitor cells. Step 1: these become osteoblasts and build two ridges of bone on either side of a small blood vessel running along the surface, creating a groove. Step 2: the ridges meet and fuse over the vessel, converting the groove into a tunnel; the periosteal lining trapped inside is now endosteum. Step 3: osteoblasts from that endosteum lay concentric rings (lamellae) inward until only a narrow central canal remains around the vessel: a new osteon, the basic cylinder of compact bone. Step 4: meanwhile osteoblasts under the periosteum keep adding circumferential lamellae, and the cycle repeats over new vessels. At the same time osteoclasts on the endosteum enlarge the medullary cavity from inside, so the wall thickens only modestly.

basics: Adult bone is not a finished structure; it is continually taken apart and rebuilt in small patches, about 5% of the skeleton at any moment. Two cell types run the cycle. Osteoclasts, large multinucleate cells, seal themselves against a bone surface and pump acid and protein-digesting enzymes into the pocket, dissolving mineral and collagen and passing the calcium into the blood: this is resorption. Osteoblasts then move into the pit and deposit fresh matrix that mineralises: deposition. Balanced, the two keep bone mass constant while replacing tired, micro-cracked material with new, tougher bone; remodeling also lets bone thicken where it is loaded and thin where it is not, and reshapes bone after injury. Rates vary enormously by site. The balance is tilted by mechanical strain, diet (calcium, phosphorus, vitamins A, C, D) and hormones (growth hormone via IGFs, thyroid hormones, insulin, sex hormones, parathyroid hormone, calcitonin); when resorption wins for years, the result is osteoporosis.

title: Repairment of bones

refs.section_title: Fracture and Repair of Bone

basics: A fracture is any break in a bone, and healing follows the logic of any wound: stop the bleeding, bridge the gap with quick provisional tissue, then replace it with the proper material. Reactive phase: torn vessels bleed into the break, forming a clot (fracture hematoma) within hours; nearby bone cells die from lack of blood, and inflammation brings phagocytes and osteoclasts to clear the debris. Reparative phase, part 1: fibroblasts and chondroblasts from the periosteum grow into the clot and lay down collagen and fibrocartilage, producing a soft fibrocartilaginous callus that splints the ends (about three weeks). Part 2: near healthy, well-supplied bone, osteoblasts convert the callus to spongy bone, the hard bony callus, lasting three to four months. Remodeling phase: osteoclasts remove dead fragments and excess callus, compact bone replaces spongy bone at the surface, and the shape is restored, often leaving only a slight thickening. Healing is slow because mineral is deposited gradually and bone cells divide slowly.

basics: Bone mass is a running balance: deposition by osteoblasts minus resorption by osteoclasts. Through childhood the balance is positive, in young adults roughly zero, and in later life negative. Osteoporosis ('porous bone') is the state in which years of net loss have thinned the trabeculae of spongy bone and the walls of compact bone so much that ordinary loads, sitting down hard or a minor fall, fracture the hip, wrist or vertebrae. The calcium ledger drives it: more calcium leaves in urine, faeces and sweat than the gut absorbs, and the skeleton, the body's calcium store, is drawn down to keep blood calcium normal. Women are affected about four times as often because their bones are smaller to begin with and because estrogen, which restrains osteoclasts and stimulates osteoblasts, falls sharply at menopause, whereas testosterone in men declines only slowly. Diagnosis is by bone mineral density scan; prevention rests on calcium, vitamin D and weight-bearing exercise, treatment on drugs that inhibit osteoclasts or stimulate osteoblasts.

basics: Calcium ions do far more than harden bone: nerves, muscles, blood clotting and many enzymes need the plasma concentration held in a narrow band (about 9-11 mg per 100 mL). Bone, holding 99% of body calcium, is the reservoir that buffers that level. The main controller is parathyroid hormone (PTH) from four small glands behind the thyroid. When blood calcium falls, parathyroid cells raise their internal cyclic AMP, a second messenger that relays the signal to the PTH gene, and secrete more PTH. PTH then (1) activates osteoclasts to resorb bone and release calcium, (2) makes the kidneys reclaim calcium instead of excreting it, and (3) stimulates the kidneys to make calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D, which increases gut absorption. Blood calcium rises and the stimulus switches off: negative feedback. Calcitonin, from the thyroid, does the opposite by inhibiting osteoclasts, though its everyday importance in humans is doubtful.

basics: About three weeks after fertilisation the embryo is a flat disc that reorganises into three sheets, the primary germ layers: ectoderm outside (future skin surface and nervous system), endoderm inside (gut lining) and mesoderm between. Almost all bone, cartilage, muscle and blood comes from mesoderm, via a loose embryonic connective tissue called mesenchyme. In the middle of week 4 small bumps appear on the flanks of the trunk, the upper limb buds, followed two days later by the lower; each is a core of mesenchyme covered by ectoderm. By week 6 a constriction sets off flattened hand and foot plates; by week 7 arm, forearm and hand (thigh, leg, foot) are distinguishable; by week 8 shoulders, elbows and wrists exist and the buds are called limbs. Inside, the mesenchyme has already condensed into cartilage models, and endochondral ossification begins by the end of week 8, with primary centres in most limb bones by week 12 and secondary centres mostly after birth.

basics: A skeleton alone is a set of levers; muscles are the motors that pull on them. Skeletal muscle is the striated, voluntary type attached to bone by tendons, and there are several hundred named muscles. Contraction can shorten a muscle to move a bone, or hold it at constant length to stabilise a joint and keep you upright; posture is continuous low-level contraction. Ring-shaped muscles (sphincters) guard openings such as the mouth, anus and bladder outlet, though Tortora notes most sphincters are smooth muscle. Because contraction is only about a quarter efficient, most of the chemical energy used appears as heat, which keeps body temperature up and is why you shiver when cold. Skeletal muscle is also the largest consumer of glucose after a meal, so it is a lever on blood sugar, a point the slide includes but Tortora's list does not. Bones, joints and muscles together are the musculoskeletal system, the province of orthopaedics.

title: Movements at synovial joints

refs.section_title: Types of Movements at Synovial Joints
refs.capture: p.276: left column bottom, section 9.5 objective and opening paragraph (the four categories), heading 'Gliding' (start 'Gliding is a simple movement') continuing in the right column; right column heading 'Angular Movements' and sub-heading 'Flexion, Extension, and Lateral Flexion', continuing p.277 (left column bulleted examples; right column lateral flexion and hyperextension; sub-heading 'Abduction, Adduction, and Circumduction' at bottom right) continuing p.278 both columns; p.278 right column heading 'Rotation' continuing p.279 left column top; p.279 left column heading 'Special Movements' with the bulleted list running down the right column to p.280 (opposition); Figures 9.4-9.9 on pp.276-280 photograph each movement; p.280 Table 9.1 'Summary of Movements at Synovial Joints' (lower page) - the slide is a condensation of this table

basics: A synovial joint is one where the bone ends are covered in cartilage and separated by a lubricated, fluid-filled cavity, so they slide freely; every limb joint is of this type. Movement vocabulary describes what happens to the angle and orientation of the bones, always starting from the anatomical position. Gliding: flat surfaces slip over each other with almost no change of angle (the small wrist and ankle bones). Angular: the angle between bones changes; flexion decreases it, extension restores it, hyperextension goes beyond the normal range; abduction moves a part away from the body's midline, adduction brings it back; circumduction is flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in sequence, tracing a cone. Rotation: a bone spins about its own long axis (medial or lateral in the limbs). 'Special' movements have their own names because only certain joints do them: elevation/depression and protraction/retraction of jaw and shoulder, inversion/eversion of the sole, dorsiflexion/plantar flexion of the ankle, pronation/supination of the forearm, opposition of the thumb.

title: Lever system and leverage

refs.section_title: How Skeletal Muscles Produce Movements - Lever Systems and Leverage

basics: A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point, the fulcrum, when a force (the effort) acts on it against a resistance (the load). In the body the bar is a bone, the fulcrum is the joint, the effort is the pull of a muscle at its insertion, and the load is the weight of the body part plus anything it carries. Torque is force times distance from the fulcrum, so the effort-arm to load-arm ratio sets the trade-off: a long effort arm gives mechanical advantage (small force, big load, slow); a short one gives mechanical disadvantage but speed and range. Levers are classed by the order of fulcrum, effort and load. First class (fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw): the head nodding on the atlas. Second class (load in the middle, like a wheelbarrow): standing on tiptoe. Third class (effort in the middle, like tweezers): the biceps flexing the elbow, the commonest arrangement in the body, sacrificing force for speed and reach.

terms.d: A rigid bar that pivots about a fixed point; in the body, a bone.

title: Skeletal muscle attachment and movements

refs.section_title: How Skeletal Muscles Produce Movements - Muscle Attachment Sites: Origin and Insertion
refs.capture: p.345 right column, heading 'Muscle Attachment Sites: Origin and Insertion', 2 paragraphs (start 'Together, the voluntarily controlled muscles') defining origin (stationary bone) and insertion (movable bone) with the door-spring analogy, continuing to the top of p.346 left column (origin usually proximal, insertion distal; belly; actions; reverse muscle action; muscles cross the joints they move); p.345 Figure 11.1 (a) origin and insertion of biceps and triceps, (b) forearm lever - the slide's figure

basics: A skeletal muscle is a bundle of contractile fibres with a tendon at each end. When it shortens it pulls its two attachments toward each other, but the two bones rarely move equally: one is held still by other muscles or by its own bulk. The attachment on the bone that stays put is the origin; the attachment on the bone that moves is the insertion; the fleshy middle is the belly. In the limbs the origin is usually proximal (nearer the trunk) and the insertion distal, and the insertion is pulled toward the origin. The slide's figure shows the biceps brachii arising from the scapula and inserting on the radius, and the triceps inserting on the olecranon of the ulna, so the belly of a muscle typically lies over the bone above the joint it moves, not over the bone it moves. A muscle must cross a joint to move it; some cross two. Origin and insertion can swap roles when the 'moving' bone is fixed, as in a pull-up (reverse muscle action).

terms.d: The tendon attachment of a muscle to the bone that stays stationary.

title: The Integumentary System performs a variety of functions for the human body. It:

refs.section_title: Functions of the Skin
refs.capture: p.164: left column, section 5.4 objective and the paragraph listing the six functions (start 'Now that you have a basic'), then headings 'Thermoregulation', 'Blood Reservoir', 'Protection' (left column, continuing right column top), 'Cutaneous Sensations' and 'Excretion and Absorption' (right column); p.165 left column, heading 'Synthesis of Vitamin D' (1 paragraph, below the Clinical Connection box)

basics: The integumentary system is the skin plus its hair, nails and glands: a two-layer sheet (thin cellular epidermis over thick fibrous dermis) resting on a fatty subcutaneous layer. Its functions follow from being the boundary with the outside world. As a barrier, its keratin-filled surface cells, waterproofing lipids, acidic sweat and pigment melanin resist abrasion, chemicals, microbes, water loss and ultraviolet light, and resident immune cells (dendritic cells, macrophages) flag invaders. As a radiator, it adjusts heat loss by sweating and by widening or narrowing dermal blood vessels, which also make the dermis a sizeable blood reservoir. As a sense organ, it carries receptors for touch, pressure, vibration, temperature and pain. It excretes a little water, salt and urea in sweat. Ultraviolet light in the epidermis converts a cholesterol derivative into a vitamin D precursor, which liver and kidney finish as calcitriol, the link to bone, since calcitriol drives intestinal calcium absorption.

title: Integumentary system and the rule of 9s

refs.section_title: Disorders: Homeostatic Imbalances - Burns (rule of nines)
refs.capture: p.172 right column, the paragraph starting 'The seriousness of a burn is determined', ending with the sentence introducing the rule of nines, followed by the numbered list 1-5 (head and neck 9%, each upper limb 9%, trunk 36%, each lower limb 18%, perineum 1%); p.173 left column Figure 5.10 'Rule-of-nines method' - the labelled body diagram; the burn-classification paragraphs (first-, second-, third-degree) and Figure 5.9 are on p.172 left column and bottom

basics: A burn destroys skin proteins, and once the barrier is gone the main dangers are systemic: plasma leaks from the burned surface, causing dehydration and shock, and microbes get in. How much fluid to replace intravenously depends on how much skin is gone, so clinicians need a fast estimate of the burned fraction of total body surface area. The rule of nines divides the adult body into regions each worth 9% or a multiple: head and neck 9%, each whole upper limb 9%, front of trunk 18% and back 18%, each whole lower limb 18%, perineum 1%, summing to 100%. Front and back of a region are each half its value, so a burn of the front of one arm is 4.5%. Proportions differ in children (larger head, smaller legs), which is why paediatric charts modify the figures. Severity also depends on depth (first-, second-, third-degree), site and the patient's age.

terms.d: The skin and its accessory structures: hair, nails, glands.
The whole skin area; burns are expressed as a percentage of it.
